**(p. 554)** Surat al-Shu'ara' is Meccan, and it has two hundred and twenty-seven verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ta-Sin-Mim﴾. The letters are pronounced *Ta Sin*, *Ya Sin*, and *Ha Mim*. They are read with *imala* (the inclination of the vowel toward the *ya* sound). This applies to the Kufan readers, except al-A'sha, al-Barjami, and Hafs. Yazid and Hamza pronounce the *nun* clearly (*izhar*) before the *mim*. The others assimilate it into the *mim* (*idgham*).

﴿These are the verses of the Book that makes things clear﴾: its inimitability (i'jaz) is evident, and it is manifest that it is from Allah. What is meant by "the Book" is the surah or the Qur'an. The meaning is: these are the verses of this composition made of the letters laid out, [namely] "These are the verses of the Clear Book."

Translation:

﴿Perhaps you will kill yourself (bākhi‘un)﴾ — qātil (killing). And "la‘alla" here expresses concern (al-ishfāq). ﴿Yourself﴾ — from grief; that is: be concerned for yourself lest you destroy it out of anguish (ḥasrah) and sorrow over what you have missed of your people's accepting Islam, ﴿that they may not be believers﴾ — lest they believe, or because of the impossibility of their faith, or out of fear that they will not believe.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 4:

﴿If We wished﴾ (i.e., their faith), ﴿We would send down upon them from the sky a sign﴾ (i.e., a clear proof), ﴿so that their necks would remain bowed to it﴾ (i.e., "so that they remain"; the conditional clause here takes a past-tense verb in the sense of the future, because the response (jaza') is expressed with a past form meaning the future. You say: "If you visit me, I will honour you," meaning "I will honour you." This is what al-Zajjaj said), ﴿their necks﴾ (meaning their leaders, their foremost ones, or their groups; it is said: "a 'unuq (group) of people came to us," meaning a company of them), ﴿bowed in submission to it﴾ (i.e., submissive). It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it was revealed concerning us and the Banu Umayyah: then dominion will be ours over them, and their necks will be humbled before us after their hardness, and humiliation will overtake them after their might.

Our'anic quotation: ﴿And there does not come to them any new reminder from the Most Merciful, but they turn away from it.﴾

Commentary: i.e., whenever Allah renews for them a admonition and reminder through His revelation, they only renew their turning away from it and their disbelief in it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 6:

﴿So they have denied⦆ Muhammad (ﷺ) in what he brought them. ﴿So there will come to them﴾, i.e. they will come to know, ﴿the news⦆, i.e. the reports, ﴿of that at which they used to mock﴾. This is a threat to them and a warning that they will come to know, when the punishment of Allah touches them, on the Day of Badr, or on the Day of Resurrection, what the thing was that they used to mock. It is the Qur'an. ﴿And there will come to them its news﴾, i.e. its reports and its circumstances, which were hidden from them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 7:

﴿Have they not seen the earth, how many of every noble kind We have caused to grow therein?﴾ "Kam" (how many) is in the accusative, governed by "anbatna" (We caused to grow). ﴿Of every kind⌋ (zawj)﴾ means a type (sinf) of vegetation. ﴿Noble﴾ means praiseworthy, abundant in benefit, from which people and livestock eat, like the noble man whose benefit is general. The benefit of combining the two words of multiplicity and comprehensiveness is that the word "kull" (every) indicates encompassing all the pairs of plants in detail, while "kam" (how many) indicates that this encompassing is abundant and exceedingly multiplied, and by this He drew attention to the perfection of His power.

Verse 8 of Surah 26 (al-Shu'ara'): ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them are not believers.﴾ That is: indeed in the growing of those various kinds (of plants) is a sign that the One who causes them to grow is able to bring the dead to life. And Allah knew that most of them are those whose hearts are sealed, whose faith is not to be hoped for.

﴿Indeed, your Lord is the Mighty﴾ in His retribution against the disbelievers, ﴿the Merciful﴾ to those among them who believe. [The verse says] "āyatan" (آيَةً, a sign) in the singular, although the sense is of many signs, because the demonstrative "dhālika" (ذَلِكَ, that) refers to the verbal noun of "anbatnā" (أَنْبَتْنا, We caused to grow). The meaning is that in each one of those pairs there is a sign, what a sign!

﴿And﴾ is an object (maf'ul bihi), meaning: remember ﴿when﴾ ﴿your Lord called out﴾, that is, called (da'a) ﴿to Musa: Go﴾. ﴿An﴾ here means "that" (i.e., "namely"),

﴿to the wrongdoing people﴾, who wronged themselves through disbelief, and the Children of Israel (Banu Isra'il) through enslavement and the slaughter of their sons. He recorded upon them the wrongdoing, then used ʿaṭf (coordination, conjoining the next clause to what came before).

﴿The people of Pharaoh﴾ is in apposition to "the wrongdoers" as an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf al-bayān), as if the meaning of "the people" is "the wrongdoers," and its restatement (tarjamatuhu) is "the people of Pharaoh." It is as if the two are expressions following one another with a single meaning. ﴿Will they not be mindful?﴾ That is: come to them as a warner, for it is time for them to be mindful. It is a word of urging and incitement. It may also be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "the wrongdoers," meaning: they wrong while not being mindful of God and His punishment, so the interrogative hamza of denunciation (hamzat al-inkār) was placed before the circumstantial clause. (p-556)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 12:

﴿He said: "My Lord, I fear that they will deny me."﴾ Fear (al-khawf) is a distress that befalls a person over a matter that is yet to occur. ﴿That they will deny me.﴾

**"And my breast tightens"** at their denying me. It is either a new, independent clause (*mustaʾnaf*, a resumed sentence) or conjoined (*ʿatf*) to **أخافُ** ("I fear").

**"And my tongue does not speak freely"**, because zeal overcomes me at what I see of the impossible and hear of the disputation. With the verbs in the subjunctive, Yaʿqub reads them as conjoined (*ʿatf*) to **"يُكَذِّبُونِ"** ("they deny me"). On this reading the fear relates to all three things. On the nominative reading, the fear relates to the denial alone.

**"So send [word] to Harun."** That is, send Gabriel to him and make him a prophet who will help me in the mission. Harun was in Egypt when Musa was sent as a prophet in al-Sham. This request from Musa, peace be upon him, was not a hesitation in carrying out the command. Rather, it was a request for help in conveying the message, and a preparing of an excuse in asking for a helper to carry out the order. It is not a hesitation in obeying the command. Asking for help is sufficient evidence of acceptance, not of making excuses.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 14:

﴿And they have a charge of sin against me⦆ That is, the consequence (tab'a) of a sin, namely the killing of the Copt; the word "consequence" (mudaf) has been elided, or he called the consequence of the sin "a sin," just as he called the recompense of an evil deed "an evil deed." ﴿So I fear that they will kill me﴾ That is, that they will kill me in retaliation for it (qisas). This is not also an excuse; rather, it is a seeking of protection against the anticipated calamity, and a fear lest he be killed before delivering the message. For this reason He promised him protection and defense with the word "No!" (kalla), and He combined both responses for him in His saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 15:

﴿He said, "Never! So go, both of you.﴾ Because (Musa) had asked Him to ward off their harm from him, Allah promised him the warding off by turning them back from fear. And (Musa) sought from Him the message of his brother, so He answered him with His words "go" — meaning, I have made him a messenger with you. "So go" is conjoined to the verb that is indicated by "never" (kalla), as if it were said: "Desist, O Musa, from what you suppose, so go, you and Harun." ﴿With Our signs﴾ — along with Our signs, which are the hand and the staff and other than these. ﴿Indeed, We are with you﴾ — meaning, with you both by way of aid and support, and with the one to whom you are sent, by knowledge and power. ﴿Listening﴾ is the predicate of "inna," or they are two predicates, meaning: hearing. And "istima'" (listening) in other than this context means: attentive hearkening to what is heard. One says "istama'a fulan hadithahu," meaning he gave ear to his speech. It is not permissible to carry it here upon that, so it is taken to mean hearing.  (p-557)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 16:

﴿So go, both of you, to Pharaoh and say: Indeed, we are the messenger of the Lord of the worlds.﴾ "Messenger" (rasul) is not made dual here as it is in His words ﴿Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord﴾ [Ta-Ha: 47], because rasul can be used with the meaning of "one who is sent" (mursal) and with the meaning of "mission" (risala). In the verse of Ta-Ha it is taken to mean "one who is sent," so it had to be made dual. Here it is taken to mean "mission," so the word applies equally to the singular, the dual and the plural when used as a description. Also, because the two of them are united and agreed upon one single law, they are as if they were one messenger; or it is meant that each one of us [is a messenger].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 17:

﴿An arsil﴾ means "send," with the word "messenger" (rasul) being taken to include the meaning of "sending" (irsal), and it also carries the meaning of "saying" (qawl). ﴿Ma'anā Banī Isrā'īl﴾ means: release them so that they may go with us to Palestine. It was their dwelling place. The two of them came to his gate, but they were not admitted for a year, until the doorkeeper said: "Here is a man who claims that he is the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds." He said: "Admit him, perhaps we shall laugh at him." So they conveyed the message to him, and Pharaoh recognised Moses, and at that point...

Pharaoh said: ﴿Did we not raise you among us as a child?﴾ The words "and you came, the two of you, to Pharaoh and said" have been omitted for brevity. Al-walid means the young child, because of how recently he had been born. The meaning is: "Were you not a little child, and did we not raise you?" ﴿And you stayed among us for years of your life﴾. It was said: thirty years.

﴿And you did your deed which you did﴾, meaning the killing of the Copt, [and] he alluded to it, since he (Pharaoh) was a king. ﴿And you are among the disbelievers﴾ in My blessing, when you killed my baker; or [it means] you were upon our religion, which you call disbelief. This is a false accusation by him against Moses, because he (Moses) was protected from disbelief, and he used to live among them by way of taqiyya (dissimulation).

ﷻ﴿He said, "I did it then, when I was among those who had gone astray."﴾ That is: at that time (إذْ ذاكَ). ﴿And I was among the misguided﴾, i.e., the ignorant (الجاهِلِينَ) of the fact that it would lead to killing. The one who is "ḍāll" (astray) from something is the one who has gone away from knowledge of it, or the forgetful (الناسِينَ), from His saying: ﴿that if one of them errs, the other will remind her﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]. So he removed from himself the attribute of disbelief, and placed "the misguided" (الضالِّينَ) in the position of "the disbelievers" (الكافِرِينَ). "Idhan" (إذًا) is both a response (jawāb) and a conditional consequence (jazā'), together. This statement came as a response to Pharaoh and as a consequence to him, because Pharaoh's saying "and you did your deed" (وفَعَلْتَ فَعْلَتَكَ) means: "you repaid my favor by what you did." So Moses said to him, "Yes" (نَعَمْ) — (p-558) "I did it, repaying you" (فَعَلْتُها مُجازِيًا لَكَ), accepting his statement, because his favor was deserving of being repaid with something like that recompense.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 21:

﴿So I fled from you﴾ to Madyan, ﴿when I feared you﴾ that you would kill me. This was when a believing man from the family of Pharaoh said to him, ﴿Indeed, the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you, so leave﴾ [al-Qasas: 20], and the rest of the verse. ﴿Then my Lord granted me judgment﴾ meaning prophethood and knowledge, so ignorance and error departed from me. ﴿And made me one of the messengers﴾ from among His messengers.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 22:

﴿And this is a favour you claim to bestow upon me, that you have enslaved the Children of Israel.﴾ He repeated his reproach of Pharaoh's claim of favour upon him, by raising him (Moses) through upbringing, and so nullified it at its root. He refused that his favour be called anything but a calamity (niqmah), since he (Moses) made clear that the true reality of Pharaoh's bounty toward him was the enslavement of the Children of Israel. This is because their enslavement, and his intention to slaughter their sons, was the cause of Moses coming into his household and being raised there. Had he left them alone, his parents would have raised him. So it is as though Pharaoh was claiming a favour upon Moses through the enslavement of his people and the removal of him from the custody of his two parents, when you examine it. And "taʿbid" (enslavement) means subjugating them and making them slaves.

He used the singular pronoun in ﴿tamunnuhā﴾ and ﴿ʿabbadta﴾, and the plural in ﴿minkum﴾ and ﴿khiftukum﴾, because the fear and the flight were not from him alone, but from him and his community (milla), who conspired to kill him. This is evidenced by His saying ﴿Indeed, the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you﴾ [al-Qasas: 20]. As for the favour, it came from him alone, and likewise the enslavement.

﴿Tilka⁠﴾ is a pointer to a vile, vague trait, which one does not know what it is until it is explained. The position of ﴿an ʿabbadta﴾ is in the nominative as an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to ﴿tilka⁠﴾, meaning: your enslaving of the Children of Israel is a favour you claim to bestow upon me.

Pharaoh said, "And what is the Lord of the worlds?" (﴿قالَ فِرْعَوْنُ وما رَبُّ العالَمِينَ﴾). That is: you claim that you are the messenger of the Lord of the worlds, so what is His attribute (ṣifah)? For when you want to ask about the attribute of Zayd, you say, "What is Zayd?" meaning: Is he tall or short? Is he a jurist (faqīh) or a physician (ṭabīb)? This was expressly stated by the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Kashshāf, al-Zamakhshari) and others.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 24:

﴿Said﴾ Musa, answering him in accordance with his question: ﴿"The Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them"﴾, i.e., and whatever is between the two kinds. ﴿"If you are certain"﴾, i.e., if you know things (p-559) through proof, then the creation of these things suffices as proof. Or: if it is hoped from you that you attain the certainty (iqan) that correct reflection (nazar) leads to, then this answer benefits you; otherwise it would not benefit you. And iqan (certainty): the knowledge that is acquired through inference (istidlal), and for this reason it is not said that Allah is muqin (certain).

Pharaoh said to those around him (﴿Said﴾, i.e., Pharaoh, ﴿to those around him﴾) from among the nobles of his people, who were five hundred men wearing bracelets of gold, which were reserved for kings only: ﴿Do you not listen?﴾ mocking his people at his response, because they claim that the two (Lord of the heavens and the earth, and Moses's Lord) are eternal, and they deny that the two are originated, and that they have a Lord. So Moses had to reason from what they had witnessed of its origination and its perishing, and so he reasoned, when...

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 26:

﴿He said: "Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers of old."﴾ That is: He is the Creator of you and the Creator of your forefathers. So if you do not take evidence from others, then take it from yourselves. And he said "the Lord of your forefathers" only because Pharaoh used to claim lordship over the people of his own age, not over those who came before them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 27:

﴿Qāla﴾ (He said), i.e., Pharaoh: ﴿Inna rasūlakumu lladhī ursila ilaykum la-majnūn﴾ ("Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is surely a madman"), inasmuch as he claims that there is in existence a god other than me. Pharaoh used to deny the divinity (ilāhiyya) of anyone other than himself.

Qur'anic quotations and the commentary's remarks are in the translation below; the quoted verse is in ﴿ ﴾ markers.

﴿He said, "Lord of the east and the west and whatever is between them, if you were to reason."﴾ Meaning: then you would draw inference from what I say and thereby know your Lord. This is the utmost of guidance, for he first generalized with the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, then, for the sake of clarification, he particularized from the general his own selves and their fathers, because the closest of what the rational person contemplates is his own self, and whoever was born of him, and what he has witnessed of his own states from the time of his birth to the time of his death. Then he particularized the east and the west, because the rising of the sun from one of the two horizons and its setting in the other, according to a straight measure through the seasons of the year and an even reckoning, is among the most evident of what one can use as proof. And because of its evidence, the Friend of the Most Merciful (Khalil al-Rahman, i.e., Abraham) turned to argue with it, rather than with giving life and causing death, against Nimrod ibn Kan'an. It is also said that Pharaoh asked him about the quiddity (al-mahiyyah, the essence or whatness of God), being ignorant of the reality of his own question. When Musa answered with the reality of the answer, it occurred to Pharaoh that Musa had deviated from the answer, since he asked about the quiddity while Musa was answering about His lordship and the signs of His workmanship. So he said, marveling at them over Musa's answer, "Do you not listen?" (p-560). Musa returned to a statement like his first, so Pharaoh called him mad, claiming that he had deviated from the answer. Then he returned a third time to a statement like his first, clarifying that the true Unity is known only through its attributes, and that asking about the quiddity is impossible. To this is the allusion in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿if you were to reason﴾, meaning: if you have intellect, it would teach you that He cannot be known except by this way. When Pharaoh was bewildered and was not able to repel the manifestation of the signs of His workmanship...

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 29:

﴿He said: "If you take a god other than me"﴾ i.e., other than me as a god. ﴿I will surely make you among those imprisoned﴾ i.e., I will surely make you one of those whose condition you have come to know in my prisons. It was his practice that whoever he wished to imprison, he would seize and throw into a pit extending deep into the earth, of great depth, alone, where he could neither see nor hear. That was worse than killing. Had he said "I will surely imprison you" (la-usjununnaka), it would not have conveyed this meaning, even though it is shorter.

﴿He said: "Even if I brought you something clear?"﴾ The waw here is for the circumstantial (hal) sense, and the interrogative hamza has entered upon it. The meaning is: "Will you do this to me even though I have come to you with something clear?" ﴿with something clear﴾, i.e., bringing a miracle (mu'jizah).

He said, "Then bring it, [the thing] that makes clear your truthfulness, if you are among the truthful," meaning that you have a clear proof. The response of the conditional clause (جَوابُ الشَرْطِ, *jawab al-shart*) is omitted, and the sense is: "then produce it."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 32:

﴿So he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a clearly visible serpent.﴾ Its serpent-ness was manifest, with nothing resembling a serpent, as is the case with things falsified by sleight of hand and magic. It is narrated that the staff rose into the sky a distance of a mile, then descended, coming toward Pharaoh, and it began to say, "O Musa, command me with whatever you wish." And Pharaoh said, "I ask you by the One who sent you to take it," so he took it, and it returned to being a staff.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 33:

﴿And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the onlookers.﴾ In this is evidence that its whiteness was something that gathered spectators to look at it, because it departed from the norm, and its whiteness was luminous. It is narrated that when Pharaoh saw the first sign, he said: "Is there anything other than it?" So Moses drew out his hand and said to Pharaoh: "What is this?" Pharaoh said: "Your hand." Then he put it into his armpit and drew it out, and it had a radiance that nearly blinds the eyes and fills the horizon.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 34:

﴿Qāla﴾ i.e., Pharaoh, ﴿to the chiefs around him﴾. It is in the accusative in two respects: an accusative in wording (lafz), and the governing element (ʿāmil) for it is what is understood within the adverbial expression (al-ẓarf); and an accusative in position (maḥall), which is the accusative of circumstance (ḥāl) from "al-malaʾ" (the chiefs), i.e., "being around him." Its governing element is "he said," ﴿Indeed, this is a knowing sorcerer﴾ in sorcery. Then he incited his people against Moses by his saying.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 35:

﴿Yurīdu an yukhrijakum min arḍikum bi-siḥrihi fa-mādhā﴾ is in the accusative (manṣūb) because it is a direct object (maf'ūl bihi), from your saying "amartuka al-khayra" (I commanded you the good). ﴿Ta'murūna﴾ means: you advise (tushīrūna) concerning his affair, by imprisonment or killing, from al-mu'āmara (conspiring), which is al-mushāwara (consultation); or from al-amr (command), which is the opposite of al-nahy (prohibition). When Pharaoh was bewildered by the sight of the two signs, the mention of his claim to divinity slipped from him, and the pride of lordship was lowered from his shoulders, and his muscles trembled from fear. He began to consult his people, who, in his own assumption, were his slaves while he was their god; or he made them the ones who command and himself the one commanded.

ſ﴿They said: "Put him off, and his brother, and send into the cities gatherers,"﴾ — أخِّرْ أمْرَهُما (Akhkhir amrahuma): postpone their matter, and do not hasten to kill them out of fear of sedition (fitnah). ﴿وابْعَثْ في المَدائِنِ حاشِرِينَ﴾ (wab'ath fi'l-madā'in ḥāshirīn): send police officers (shuraṭ) who will gather the sorcerers. And they (the scholars of the Arabic-language tradition) set the phrase "إنَّ هَذا لَساحِرٌ عَلِيمٌ" (Inna hadhā la-sāḥirun ʿalīm, "Indeed, this is a knowing sorcerer") against Pharaoh's statement, by their words.
﴿They will bring you every skilled sorcerer who is learned﴾. So they used the word of comprehensiveness and the intensive form, so as to calm some of his anxiety.

The commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 38:

﴿So the magicians were gathered for the appointment of a known day﴾. That is, the day of the adornment (yawm al-zinah), and its appointed time (miqat) was the time of forenoon (duha), because it was the time that Musa (peace be upon him) set for them on the day of the adornment, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your appointment is the day of the adornment, and that the people be gathered at forenoon﴾ [Ta-Ha: 59]. And the miqat (appointed time, term) is that which is fixed (wuqqita), i.e., determined, of time or of place, and from it come the mawaqit al-ihram (the designated places at which pilgrims must assume the state of ihram).

(p-562)

﴿And it is said to the people: "Are you assembled?"﴾ That is, "Assemble." It is an istibṭā' (an expression of impatience at their slowness) concerning their gathering, and what is meant by it is their being hurried, their being hurried.

Qur'an 26:40: "Perhaps we shall follow the sorcerers in their religion, if they are the victorious."

That is: they had been victorious over Musa in his religion. Their real aim was not to follow the sorcerers, but the overall aim was that they should not follow Musa. So the speech was framed as a kinayah (an allusive expression, where the stated meaning points to an intended meaning), because if they followed the sorcerers, they would not be following Musa.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verses 41–42:

﴿He said: "Yes, and you will indeed be among those brought near."﴾ And it is read with a kasra on the ʿayn (ʿalī, i.e. مِنَ المُقَرِّبِينَ), and both are dialectal variants (lughatān). That is: Pharaoh said, "Yes, you will have a reward from me, and in addition to that you will be among those brought near to me in rank and station, so that you will be the first to enter upon me and the last to leave me."

Since their saying ﴿Will we surely have a reward?﴾ carries the meaning of the conditional response (jazāʾ al-sharṭ), because it indicates it, and since his saying ﴿and you will indeed be among those brought near﴾ is conjoined to it (maʿṭūfan ʿalayhi), idhan (then, in that case) remained fixed in its place, the place that the answer and the response require of it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verses 41–42:

﴿He said: "Yes, and you will indeed be among those brought near."﴾ And it is read with a kasra on the ʿayn (ʿalī, i.e. مِنَ المُقَرِّبِينَ), and both are dialectal variants (lughatān). That is: Pharaoh said, "Yes, you will have a reward from me, and in addition to that you will be among those brought near to me in rank and station, so that you will be the first to enter upon me and the last to leave me."

Since their saying ﴿Will we surely have a reward?﴾ carries the meaning of the conditional response (jazāʾ al-sharṭ), because it indicates it, and since his saying ﴿and you will indeed be among those brought near﴾ is conjoined to it (maʿṭūfan ʿalayhi), idhan (then, in that case) remained fixed in its place, the place that the answer and the response require of it.
﴿Moses said to them, "Throw down what you are about to throw."﴾ [That is] of the magic, for you will see its outcome.

Then they threw down their ropes, seventy thousand ropes, and their staffs, seventy thousand staffs. It is said that the ropes were seventy-two thousand, and likewise the staffs. And they said, "By the might of Pharaoh, we are surely the victors." They swore by his might and his power, and this is one of the oaths of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic Age of Ignorance).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 45:

﴿So Musa threw down his staff, and behold, it swallowed﴾ tabtali'u (swallows) ﴿what they falsely pretended﴾ ma ya'fikun: they turn it away from its face and its reality by their magic, and they falsify it, and they make it appear in their ropes and their staffs that they are snakes moving swiftly.

﴿Then the magicians were thrown down, prostrating.﴾ He expressed the prostration's falling down by the word "thrown" (ilqa'), by way of mushakalah (correspondence in wording), because it was mentioned alongside the "casting" (ilqa'at) [of their ropes and staffs], and because, owing to the speed with which they prostrated, they became as though they had been thrown down. (p-٥٦٣)
﴿They said: "We believe in the Lord of the worlds."﴾ It is related from ʿIkrimah, may Allah be pleased with him, that they became sorcerers in the morning and by evening they were martyrs.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 48:

﴿Lord of Moses and Aaron﴾ is an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) to "Lord of the worlds," because Pharaoh used to claim lordship (al-rububiyyah), so they wanted to specify and dissociate from him. It is also said that when Pharaoh heard from them, "We believe in the Lord of the worlds," he said, "You mean me," and they said, "The Lord of Moses and Aaron."

Pharaoh said: "Have you believed in him before I gave you permission? Indeed he is your chief, who taught you magic," (that is, the matter) "and you have certainly conspired together in a scheme and deceit. So you will soon know" the consequence of what you have done. Then he made it explicit and said: "I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides," because of a difference that appeared among you, "and I will surely crucify you all."

He intended by this to terrify the common people, so that they would not follow them in faith.
﴿They said: "No harm (lā ḍayra)"﴾ — lā ḍarar (no harm), and the predicate of lā is omitted, meaning: "in that" or "upon us." ﴿Indeed, we are returning to our Lord.﴾

We hope that our Lord will forgive us our sins, because we were the first of the believers" — (that is,) among the people of the assembly, or among the subjects of Pharaoh. They said: there is no harm to us in this; rather, great benefit accrues to us from enduring it for the sake of Allah's countenance, namely the expiation of sins. Or (the meaning is): there is no harm to us in what you threaten us with, for we must return to our Lord by one of the causes of death, and killing is the least of its causes and the most hopeful of them. Or (the meaning is): there is no harm to us in killing us, for if you kill us we shall return to our Lord with the return of one who hopes for His forgiveness and expects His mercy, because of the precedence in faith that He has granted us.

And We revealed to Moses: "Travel by night with My servants." The Hijazi reciters read the hamza with *waṣl* (connected, i.e., elided) [*waṣl*: the connecting of the initial hamza in running speech]. ﴿My servants﴾: the Children of Israel, whom He called His servants because of their faith in His Prophet. That is, "Travel with them by night." This was after years [had passed] since the faith of the magicians. (p-564) ﴿Indeed you will be pursued﴾: Pharaoh and his people will pursue you. He gave the reason for the command to travel by night as the pursuit of Pharaoh and his soldiers in your tracks. That is: I have arranged the plan for your affair and theirs so that you advance and they follow you until they enter your entrance point through the sea, and then I destroy them. It is narrated that on that night, in every house of theirs a child died, so they busied themselves with their dead until Moses departed with his people. It is also narrated that God Most High revealed to Moses: "Gather the Children of Israel, every four households into one house, then slaughter the young goats and smear their blood on your doors, for I will command the angels not to enter any house whose door has blood on it, and I will command them to kill the firstborn of the Copts. Bake unleavened bread, for it is quicker for you. Then travel with My servants until you reach the sea, and My command will come to you."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 53:

﴿Then Pharaoh sent heralds into the cities to gather [the people]﴾, meaning: gatherers, who would assemble the people by force. So when they had assembled, he said.

Verse 54: ﴿Indeed, these are a small band, insignificant.﴾ "Shirdhimah" is a company, a small group. He (Allah) first described them with a noun denoting paucity, then made them "qalil" (few) by an adjective, then pluralized "qalil," so that each faction of them is "qalil." He chose the sound masculine plural (jam' al-salamah, which is used for paucity) or he meant by "qillah" (paucity) humiliation (dhilla), not paucity of number. That is: because of their small number, they are not heeded, and their victory is not expected. Yet Musa's people were regarded as numerous, being six hundred thousand and seventy thousand, due to the large number of those with him. According to al-Dahhak: they were seven thousand thousand.

[Verse 26:55] "And indeed, they are enraging us"

That is: they are doing deeds that enrage us and constrict our breasts, namely their leaving our land, their carrying off our ornaments, and their killing our firstborn (abkar).

And indeed we are all vigilant (wary) — ﴿وَإنّا لَجَمِيعٌ حاذِرُونَ﴾. The reading of Ibn 'Amir (Shami) and Kufan readers is ﴿حاذِرُونَ﴾, while the others read ﴿حَذِرُونَ﴾. Al-Hadhir (حَذِر) is the one who is alert and watchful, whereas al-hadhir (حاذِر) is the one who renews his caution constantly. It was also said that al-hadhir means one who is fully equipped with weapons. He does this out of caution and precaution for himself. The meaning is: "We are a people whose habit is vigilance and caution and the exercise of prudence in affairs; so if some rebel emerges against us, we hasten to cut off his corruption." These are excuses which he offered to the people of the cities, lest he be thought to be weak and lax.
So We drove them out from gardens (basatin) and springs, and flowing rivers.

{And treasures} and apparent wealth of gold and silver, and he called them "treasures" because they do not spend from them in obedience to Allah the Exalted. {And a noble station} and dwelling, splendid and beautiful. And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, it is reported that it means pulpits.

﴿Thus﴾ may be in the accusative (nasb), meaning: "We expelled them with an expulsion like the one We have described." It may also be in the nominative (raf'), as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada', subject), meaning: "The matter is thus." ﴿And We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them.﴾ On the authority of al-Hasan: when they crossed the river, they returned and took their dwellings and their wealth.

﴿فَأتْبَعُوهُمْ﴾ means "so they overtook them" (فَلَحِقُوهم). The reading "فاتَّبَعُوهُمْ" is attributed to Yazid. ﴿مُشْرِقِينَ﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), meaning "entering the time of sunrise (shurūq al-shams), which is its rising." The Pharaoh's people overtook Musa and his people at the time of sunrise.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 61:

﴿When the two hosts saw each other﴾ i.e., they came face to face, such that each party could see its companion. The intended ones are the Children of Israel and the Copts. ﴿The companions of Moses said, "Indeed, we are going to be overtaken."﴾ i.e., our enemy is about to catch up with us, and the sea is before us.

Moses, peace be upon him, said, relying on God's promise to him: ﴿Never! Surely my Lord is with me; He will guide me.﴾ Rebuke yourselves for having bad thoughts about God; ﴿they will not overtake you.﴾ "Maʿiya" (with me): Ḥafṣ reads it with the vowelled yāʾ (ʿIyā). ﴿My Lord is with me; He will guide me﴾, meaning: He will guide me to the path of salvation from their pursuit and their harm. "Sayahdīnī" (He will guide me): Yaʿqūb reads it with the yāʾ (sayahdīnī, with the yāʾ written in full).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 63:

﴿So We revealed to Musa: "Strike the sea with your staff."﴾ That is, the Qulzum (the Red Sea) or the Nile. ﴿Then it parted﴾ — i.e., he struck it, ﴿and it split and was cleft﴾ and became twelve paths, according to the number of the tribes (asbat). ﴿And each part﴾ — i.e., each portion that separated from it — ﴿was like the great mountain﴾ — like a mountain towering up into the sky. ﴿the great﴾ (p-566)

"And We brought the others near" there (﴿وَأزْلَفْنا ثَمَّ﴾) — at the place where the sea split (حَيْثُ انْفَلَقَ البَحْرُ) — "the others" (﴿الآخَرِينَ﴾), namely the people of Pharaoh (قَوْمَ فِرْعَوْنَ). That is: We drew them near (أيْ: قَرَّبْناهم), either to the Children of Israel (مِن بَنِي إسْرائِيلَ) or to the sea (أوْ مِنَ البَحْرِ).
And We delivered Moses and those with him, all of them, from drowning.

Then We drowned the others: Pharaoh and his people. In this there is a refutation of the claim that the stars influence lifespans and other events, for they all gathered in destruction despite the differences in their ascendant signs (tawali').

It is narrated that Jibril, peace be upon him, was between the Children of Israel and the family of Pharaoh. He would say to the Children of Israel, "Let your last join your first," and he would face the Copts. He would say, "Slowly, let your last join your first." When Musa reached the sea, Yusha' said to Musa, "Where were you commanded? This sea is in front of you, and the family of Pharaoh has overtaken you." Musa said, "Here." So Yusha' plunged into the water, and Musa struck the sea with his staff, and they entered.

It is also narrated that Musa, peace be upon him, said at that moment: "O You who were before everything, O Originator of everything, O You who remain after everything."

﷿ Translation:

﴿Indeed, in that⦄ — i.e., in what We did to Musa and Fir'awn — ﴿is surely a sign⦄, a wondrous lesson that cannot be described. ﴿And most of them were not believers⦄ — i.e., most of those who were drowned. They said: none of them believed except Asiya, Hizqil (the believer of the family of Fir'awn), and Maryam, the one who showed Musa the grave of Yusuf.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 68:

﴿And indeed, your Lord is the Mighty (al-'Aziz)﴾ in exacting retribution from His enemies, ﴿the Merciful (al-Rahim)﴾ in bestowing favour upon His friends.
﴿And recite to them﴾ to the polytheists of Quraysh, ﴿the account of Abraham﴾, its news.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 70:

﴿When he said to his father and his people﴾ — either "his people" meaning the people of Ibrahim, or the people of the father. ﴿"What do you worship?"﴾ That is: "What thing is it that you worship?" Ibrahim, peace be upon him, knew that they were worshippers of idols, but he asked them in order to show them that what they worship does not deserve to be worshipped.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 71:

﴿They said: "We worship idols"﴾ — the answer to ﴿What do you worship?﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 70] is ﴿idols﴾, like ﴿They ask you what they should spend; say: the surplus﴾ [al-Baqarah 219] and ﴿What did your Lord say? They said: the truth﴾ [Saba' 23], because it is a question about the object of worship, not about the act of worship. They added "we worship" in the answer only out of pride and boasting in their worship of them, and for this reason they conjoined it with "we worship": ﴿so we remain devoted to them﴾, meaning we persist in worshipping them throughout the day. They said "fa-nazallu" (so we remain) because they used to worship them by day and not by night; or its meaning is continuity.
﴿Qāla﴾ (He said), i.e., Ibrahim: ﴿Do they hear you?﴾ Do they hear your supplication (du'a')? The noun is elided, indicated by ﴿when you call﴾ which points to it.
﴿Or do they benefit you﴾ if you worship them, ﴿or do they harm﴾ if you abandon their worship.

"They said, "Rather," — an act of turning away (idrab): meaning, they do not hear, nor benefit, nor harm, and we do not worship them for any of those things; but ﴿we found our fathers doing so﴾, so we imitated them."
﴿You and your forefathers of old﴾, the earlier ones.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 77:

﴿Indeed they﴾ — i.e., the idols — ﴿are an enemy to me﴾. The word ʿaduww (enemy) and ṣadīq (friend) may both be used in the sense of the singular and the plural. The meaning is: were I to worship them, they would be enemies to me on the Day of Resurrection, as in His saying: ﴿They will deny their worship of them and will be opposed to them﴾ [Maryam: 82]. Al-Farrāʾ (d. 207 AH) said: it is of the inverted construction (al-maqlūb), meaning: "Indeed I am their enemy." In His saying ﴿an enemy to me﴾, rather than "an enemy to you," there is an added element of sincere counsel, so that it is more likely to win their acceptance. Had He said, "Indeed they are an enemy to you" (ʿadw lakum), it would not have carried that same effect. ﴿Except the Lord of the worlds﴾ — this is an exceptive clause of the disconnected type (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), because He does not fall under the category of "enemies." It is as if he said: "But the Lord of the worlds [is no enemy]."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 78:

﴿Who created me﴾ by the act of bringing into being, in a secure dwelling, ﴿and it is He who guides me﴾ to the paths of this world and to the interests of the religion (dīn). The use of the future tense in "yahdīnī" (He will guide me), together with the prior precedence of divine care, is because it may carry the sense of "He guides me to what is most important, most excellent, and most complete." Or [the meaning is]: "Who created me for the means of His service, so He guides me to the etiquettes of His intimate friendship (khullah)."

(p-568)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 79:

﴿And He who feeds me and gives me drink﴾ He attributed the feeding to the Patron of the favour, because relying on means is the habit of the cattle (al-an'am). ﴿And gives me drink﴾. Ibn 'Ata' said: He is the One who gives me life through His food and quenches me with His drink.

"And when I am ill" — he did not say "when He makes me ill," because he intended remembrance with the tongue of gratitude, so he did not attribute to Him anything that implies harm. Ibn ʿAṭāʾ said: "And when I am ill through seeing creation, ﴿then it is He who heals me﴾ through witnessing the Truth." Al-Ṣādiq said: "When I am ill through seeing actions, then it is He who heals me by unveiling the favour of bounty."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 81:

﴿And He who causes me to die, then gives me life﴾. He did not say "when I die," because that (dying) is the exit from the prison of trial and the abode of perishing to the garden of enduring existence, for the promise of meeting (Allah). He used "thumma" (then, indicating a delay) with the giving of life, because it is distant from the causing of death. And He used "fa" (so, indicating immediate sequence) with guidance and healing, because they follow (upon) creation and sickness, not simultaneously.

﴿And the one from whom I hope﴾ is the hope of slaves in their masters for bounty, not as a right owed through asking. ﴿That He will forgive me my sin﴾. It was said that this refers to His saying, ﴿Indeed, I am sick﴾ [al-Saffat: 89], ﴿Rather, it was their chief who did it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 63], and ﴿This is my lord﴾ [al-An'am: 76], and to his saying to al-Bazigh, "She is my sister," concerning Sarah. These were only ma'arid (indirect statements, allusions) that are permissible, and they are not sins for which he asks forgiveness. The seeking of forgiveness by the prophets is humility from them before their Lord, a lowering of themselves, and instruction for the nations in seeking forgiveness. ﴿On the Day of Religion﴾ means the Day of Recompense.

Lord, grant me wisdom (ḥukman): either wisdom (ḥikmah), or judgment (ḥukm) among people with truth, or prophethood, because the Prophet ﷺ possesses both wisdom and judgment among the servants of God. ﴿And join me with the righteous﴾, that is, the prophets. God has indeed answered him, when He said: ﴿And indeed, in the Hereafter he will be among the righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:130].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 84:

﴿And appoint for me a tongue of truth among the later generations.﴾ That is: a good praise and a fine remembrance among the nations that will come after me. So I was given that, for every people of religion take him as their ally and praise him. The "tongue" has been placed in the position of "speech," because speech is done by means of it.

Ibn Kathir reports... no, this is only the passage given. Translation:

﴿And make me among﴾ "min" (among) is connected to an implied element, meaning: an inheritor from ﴿the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss﴾, i.e., among those who remain in it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 86:

﴿And forgive my father﴾ — make him one of those deserving forgiveness by granting him Islam; and his promise of Islam was on the day he parted from him (i.e., when he separated from him). ﴿Indeed he was among the misguided﴾ — the disbelievers.

﴿And do not disgrace me﴾ [Al-Qasas: 7]. Al-Ikhza' (causing disgrace) is from al-khizy, which means humiliation or disgrace, or from al-khizaya, which means shame (al-haya'). This is similar to al-istighfar (seeking forgiveness), as we explained.

﴿on the day they are resurrected﴾. The pronoun in it refers to the servants, because they are already known, or to the misguided (al-dallin). It may also be taken as part of the istighfar for his father, meaning: "Do not disgrace me on a day when the misguided are resurrected, and my father is among them."
"On the Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit" is a substitute (badal) for the first "the Day" (yawm). "Nor children" [will benefit anyone].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 89:

﴿Except for one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾, sound of disbelief and hypocrisy. The heart of the disbeliever and the hypocrite is diseased, according to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿there is a disease in their hearts﴾ [al-Baqara: 10]. That is: when wealth is spent on the paths of righteousness, and his children are righteous, then he benefits by it and by them, with a sound heart. Or, wealth and children are regarded as having the meaning of richness, as if it were said: "On the Day when neither ﴿wealth nor children will benefit﴾" except the richness of one who comes to God with a sound heart, because a man's richness in his religion is through the soundness of his heart, just as his richness in his worldly life is through his wealth and his children. The word "man" (*man*) has been made the object of "yanfa'u" (benefit), meaning: no wealth and no children benefit except a man whose heart is sound along with his wealth, in that he spent it in obedience to God, and along with his children, in that he guided them to the religion and taught them the laws (*shara'i'*). It is also permissible, on this reading, that ﴿except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ refers to [being safe] from the trial of wealth and children. The Majestic One has indeed approved the exception of Abraham, honouring him, then made it a description of him in His saying: ﴿And indeed, among his followers was Abraham﴾ [al-Saffat: 83], ﴿when he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾ [al-Saffat: 84]. How excellent was the arrangement, peace be upon him, of his speech (p-570) with the polytheists: he first asked them what they worshipped, as a question establishing a point rather than a question seeking information; then he turned to their deities and nullified their affair, showing that they do not harm, nor benefit, nor hear; and [he addressed] their imitation of their forefathers of old, removing it from being even a doubt, let alone a proof. Then he portrayed the matter within himself, apart from them, until he extricated himself from it to the mention of God, exalted is He, magnifying His standing and enumerating His blessings from the time of His originating him until the time of his death, together with what he hopes for in the Hereafter of His mercy. Then he followed that by supplicating with the supplications of the sincere, and invoked Him with the humility of good manners. Then he connected it to the mention of the Day of Resurrection, the reward and punishment of God, and what the polytheists will suffer on that day of regret and anguish over the misguidance they were in, and their wish for a return to the world that they might believe and obey.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 90:

﴿And Paradise will be brought near to the God-fearing﴾. That is: brought close. It is a conjunction of one clause to another, meaning: it will be brought near from the standing-place of the blessed, so that they will look upon it.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 91:**

﴿And Hellfire is brought forth for the deviators﴾ means: it is made manifest, until its blaze nearly seizes them. ﴿For the deviators﴾ means: for the disbelievers.

And it will be said to them: "Where is what you used to worship ﴿besides Allah? Can they help you, or help themselves?﴾" They are rebuked for their polytheism: it is said to them, "Where are your gods? Do they benefit you by their help, or do they benefit themselves by their own victory?" Because they and their gods are the fuel of the Fire.

And it will be said to them: "Where is what you used to worship ﴿besides Allah? Can they help you, or help themselves?﴾" They are rebuked for their polytheism: it is said to them, "Where are your gods? Do they benefit you by their help, or do they benefit themselves by their own victory?" Because they and their gods are the fuel of the Fire.

**Then they will be hurled headlong** (fa-kubkibu): they will be overturned and cast down, some of them upon others, **into it** (fiha), that is, into the Blazing Fire (al-Jahim), **they** (hum), that is, the false deities (al-ālihah) **and the deviators** (al-ghawun), and their worshippers, those to whom Hell was made visible (burizat lahum).

Al-kabkabah is the repetition of al-kabb (overturning, casting down). The repetition in the wording was made to indicate repetition in the meaning, as if, when they are thrown into Hell, they are overturned again and again until they settle at its bottom. We seek refuge in God from it.
Qur'an 26:95: ﴿And the hosts of Iblis, all together﴾. His devils, or those who follow him from the disobedient among mankind and the jinn.

"They will say, while they dispute therein" (﴿قالوا وهم فيها يختصمون﴾). It is permissible that God makes the idols speak, so that the mutual speech and the disputing may be valid; and it is permissible that this exchange takes place between the disobedient (sinners) and the devils.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿When we made you equal﴾ — "we make you equal" means: we place you (O idols) on a par ﴿with the Lord of the worlds﴾ in worship.

Note on the gloss: "nusawwikum" is rendered here as "we make you equal"; the commentary explains it as "naʿdilukum" (we hold you on equal footing), and the object of equality is worship (ʿibadah).
ﷻ﴿And none led us astray except the criminals﴾. That is: their leaders who misled them, or Iblis and his hosts, and whoever established polytheism (al-shirk) as a practice.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 26, verse 100:**

﴿So we have no intercessors﴾, as the believers have from among the prophets, the friends of God (*awliya'*), and the angels.

﴿Nor any close friend﴾ (26:101), as we see them as friends. In the Hereafter, only the believers are true friends with one another, whereas among the people of the Fire there is enmity. ﴿Intimate friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the God-fearing﴾ (al-Zukhruf [43]:67). Or ﴿So we have no intercessors﴾ (al-Shu'ara' [26]:100). ﴿Nor any close friend﴾ (26:101) from among those whom we used to count as intercessors and friends, because they believed that their idols were their intercessors with God. They had friends from among the devils of mankind. Al-hamim (the close friend, the one who is intimate) derives from al-ihtimam (concern), which is the concern of one who cares about what concerns you. Or it derives from al-hamma (the inner circle), meaning the intimate, the special friend. The intercessors are plural, but the friend is singular, because intercessors are usually many. As for al-sadiq (the true friend), who is the one sincere in his affection for you, who is concerned with what concerns you, he is rare. Al-Hakim (a wise man) was asked about the true friend and said: "It is a name with no meaning." It is also permissible that al-sadiq (the friend) is intended in the plural sense.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 102:

﴿Then if only we had a return (karra)﴾ — a return (raj'a) to the world — ﴿so that we would be among the believers﴾. The answer to "law" (if only) is omitted, and it is: "we would have done such-and-such and such-and-such." Or "law" in such a context carries the sense of wishing (tamanni), as if it were said: "So would that we had a return," because of the affinity between the meaning of law and laytа (would that) (in the sense of) convergence.

Indeed, in that (يعني: فيما ذُكر من الأنباء) — in what has been mentioned of the reports — is surely a sign (أي: لعبرة لمن اعتبر), that is, a lesson for whoever takes heed. "And most of them were not believers" — so it is said that a group of them did believe.

Translation:

Indeed, in that (in what has been mentioned of the accounts) there is surely a sign (that is, a lesson for whoever takes heed). "And most of them were not believers" — and so it is said that a group of them did believe.

﴿And indeed your Lord is the Mighty﴾ the Avenger against those who denied Ibrahim (Abraham) with the fire of the Blazing Hellfire (p-572) ﴿the Merciful﴾ the One who delivers every person with a sound heart to the Garden of Bliss.

Qur'an 26:105: "The people of Noah denied the messengers."

"Qawm" (people) may be treated as masculine or feminine. It was said that Noah was born in the time of Adam, peace be upon him. The parallel to His saying "the messengers" (al-mursalin), where the intended referent is Noah, peace be upon him, is your saying: "So-and-so rides beasts and wears garments (burud)," while he has only one beast or one garment. Alternatively, they denied the sending of messengers altogether, and therefore it is stated in the plural. Or, because whoever denies one of them has denied them all, since every messenger calls people to believe in all the messengers. The same applies to everything in this surah.

Translation:

﴿When their brother Noah said to them﴾ (a brother by lineage, not in religion), ﴿"Will you not fear God?"﴾ (meaning: will you not fear the Creator of mankind, so that you abandon the worship of idols).
Qur'anic quotation: ﴿Indeed, I am a trustworthy messenger to you.﴾ He was known among them for trustworthiness, just as Muhammad (ﷺ) was among the Quraysh.

Quranic quotation: ﴿So fear Allah and obey me﴾ in what I command you and call you to of the truth.

Note on the rendering: the passage is a brief gloss in al-Nasafi's Madarik al-Tanzil on Surah al-Shu'ara' 26:108. The quoted verse is rendered as above, and the gloss is translated as it stands.

﴿And I do not ask you for any reward﴾ upon this matter, ﴿any wage﴾ as recompense, ﴿if my reward﴾ (read with a fatha, أَجْرِيَ, by the Madinan, the Syrian, Abu 'Amr and Hafs) ﴿is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾. Therefore I seek it.

Quranic quotation: ﴿So fear Allah and obey me.﴾ He repeated it to establish it in their souls, with each of the two being attached to a reason. The reason for the first is that he was trustworthy among them, and the reason for the second is cutting off their greed (ḥasm ṭamaʿihi minhum), as if he said: "When you know my message and my trustworthiness, then fear Allah; then when you know my abstention from wages (ijtirāzī min al-ajr), then fear Allah."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 111:

﴿They said: "Shall we believe you, when the lowest ones have followed you?"﴾ The wāw (waw) here is for the circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and qad (قد) is implied after it. The evidence for this is the reading of Ya'qub: "wa-atbāʿuka" (وَأتْباعُكَ), the plural of tābiʿ (تابِعٌ), like shāhid (شاهِدٌ) and ashhād (أشْهادٌ), or of tabaʿ (تَبَعٌ), like baṭal (بَطَلٌ) and abṭāl (أبْطالٌ).

﴿al-arḏalūn (الأرْذَلُونَ)﴾: the base, the vile. Al-raḏālah (الرَذالَةُ) is baseness and lowliness. They called them base only because of the lowliness of their lineage and the scarcity of their share of worldly goods. It was also said that they were from the people of base crafts. But a craft does not diminish one's religion; wealth is the wealth of religion and lineage is the lineage of piety. It is not permissible to call a believer "base," even if he is the poorest of people and the lowest in lineage. The followers of the prophets have always been like this.

ﷺ — note: honorifics not present here, so none needed.

"He said, 'And what is my knowledge' (wa-ayyu shay'in 'ilmi), i.e., what knowledge do I have, '[of] what they used to do'" (bi-ma kanu ya'malun), "[namely] of the crafts (al-sina'at). I only ask of them faith (al-iman)." It is also said that they (the people of Noah) reproached him, along with their contempt for them (istirdaluhum), regarding their faith, and said: "Those who believed in you, there is not in their hearts what they show." So he said: "I am only responsible for judging by outward appearances (i'tibar al-zawahir), without searching into inner secrets (al-sara'ir)."
﴿Their reckoning is only upon my Lord, if you could perceive.﴾ That is, Allah will call them to account for what is in their hearts.
﴿Wa-ma ana bi-taridi al-mu'minin﴾ means: it is not my place to follow your desires by driving away the believers in the hope of (winning) your faith.

﴿I am but a clear warner﴾. My duty is only that I warn you with a clear warning, by means of sound proof by which truth is distinguished from falsehood. Then you yourselves know best about your own affair.

"They said: 'If you do not desist, O Noah, you will surely be among those stoned to death.'" (Qur'an 26:116)

Translation of the commentary:

"If you do not desist" from what you are saying, "you will surely be among those stoned" — i.e., among those killed by stoning.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 117:

﴿He said: "My Lord, my people have denied me."﴾ This is not a report of the denial, since He knows (that), for the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed is more knowing. Rather, he intended that they had denied me concerning Your revelation and Your message.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 118:

﴿Fa-iftah baini wa bainahum fathan﴾ means: judge between me and them with a judgment (hukman). The fataha (fatahah) is al-hukumah (judgment, adjudication), and the fattah is the judge (al-hakim), because he "opens" what is closed, just as he is called faysal (the decisive one), because he separates (yafsilu) between disputes (al-khusumat). ﴿Wa najjini wa man ma'iya﴾ — Hafs (reads it as) ﴿min al-mu'minin﴾, from the punishment of their deeds (min 'adhabi 'amalihim). (p-574)

"So We saved him and those with him in the laden ship." (Qur'an 26:119)

Al-Fulk: the ship; its plural is fulk. The singular is on the pattern of qufl, and the plural on the pattern of usud. Al-mashhun: the filled, the loaded. From it comes shihnat al-balad (the governor or garrison of a city), meaning one who fills it with sufficiency.
Then We drowned the rest after that: that is, after saving Noah and those who believed with him, [We drowned] ﴿the rest﴾ of his people.

﴿And indeed, your Lord is the Almighty﴾, the Avenger, by humiliating the one who denied and persisted in denial, ﴿the Most Merciful﴾, the Bestower of favour, by aiding the one who affirmed Oneness and acknowledged.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 123:

﴿The people of ʿĀd denied the messengers.﴾ It is a tribe, and originally it was the name of a man who was the father of the tribe.

Translation:

﴿So fear Allah﴾ regarding your denial of the trustworthy Messenger, ﴿and obey me﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 128:

﴿Do you build on every high place⁠—﴾ a landmark, a dovecote or a building which, because of its height, serves as a sign; they mock those who pass by them. ﴿Playing?⁠﴾ Amusing yourselves.

﴿And you take for yourselves fortresses﴾ (maṣāniʿ), meaning water channels (maʾākhidh al-māʾ), or lofty palaces (quṣūran mushayyadah), or fortresses (ḥuṣūnan), ﴿that you may live forever﴾, meaning you hope to remain forever in this world (tarjūna al-khulūda fī al-dunyā).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on Surah 26, verse 130:

﴿And when you seize﴾ you take [them] with the seizing of punishment. ﴿You seize as tyrants﴾: killing with the sword and beating with the whip. The *jabbar* is one who kills and strikes in anger.

Translation of the passage:

﴿So fear Allah﴾ regarding the seizing (by force), ﴿and obey me﴾ in what I call you to.
﴿And fear Him who has aided you with what you know﴾ [of] the blessings. Then He enumerated them to them, saying (p-575)
﴿Has provided you with cattle and sons﴾. He joined sons with cattle, because they assist them in guarding them and tending to them.
﴿Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day﴾ if you disobey me.

"They said: 'It is all the same to us whether you admonish or are not among those who admonish.'" That is: your speech and your call will not be accepted, whether you admonish or keep silent. He did not say "am lam ta'iz" (or you did not admonish) for the sake of the ends of verses (li-ru'us al-ayy).

ۡ**﴿Indeed, this is nothing but the custom of the earlier generations.﴾** This means: what we are upon of life and death, and of building structures, is nothing but the custom of the earlier generations; or, what we are upon is the religion of the earlier generations. "Khalqa al-awwalin" (the creation of the earlier generations) is the reading of Makki, Basri, Yazid and Ali. The meaning is: what you have brought is the fabrication (ikhtilaq) of the earlier generations and the lies of the false prophets before you, like their saying, ﴿legends of the earlier generations﴾ [al-Anfal: 31]. Or, the meaning is: our creation is like the creation of the earlier generations; we die and live as they lived.
**"And we shall not be punished"** (﴿وَما نَحْنُ بِمُعَذَّبِينَ﴾), in this world, nor is there any resurrection (ba'th) or reckoning (hisab).

ﷺ-free passage; translate faithfully.

"﴿So they denied him﴾, i.e., Hud. ﴿So We destroyed them﴾ with a furious, raging wind. ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers﴾."

Note on rendering: the verse as it appears in the passage is ﴿فَكَذَّبُوهُ فَأهْلَكْناهُمْ﴾ and the rest of the verse continues in the same quotation, so the translation follows that.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 26, verse 146:

﴿Will you be left﴾ is a denunciation of their being left to abide in their bliss, never to be removed from it, ﴿in what is here﴾, meaning in that which has settled in this place of bliss, ﴿secure﴾ from punishment, from cessation, and from death. Then he explained it with his words (p. 576)
In gardens and springs. This too is a general statement followed by detail.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 148:

﴿And fields of crops and date-palms⁠﴾ The date-palm (nakhl) is coordinated (ʿuṭifa) with "gardens" (jannāt), even though the word "garden" (jannah) already includes the date-palm, first of all. This is to give the date-palm precedence over the rest of the trees. ﴿Its spathe⁠﴾ is what emerges from the date-palm like the blade of a sword. ﴿Soft⁠﴾ means tender and ripe. It is as if he said: "And date-palms whose fruit has ripened into dates (ruṭab)."

﴿And you carve﴾ means you hollow out ﴿from the mountains, houses, skillful﴾. The reading of the Shami and Kufi (the readings of the Syrian and Kufan schools) has ﴿skillful﴾ as ḥādhiqīn, which is a ḥāl (circumstantial state, a term for a clause describing the condition of the subject at the time of the action). Others read it as "fārihīn," meaning exultant or proud. Farāha means shrewdness and energy.

﴿And do not obey the command of the extravagant﴾. [He meant] the disbelievers, or the nine men who hamstrung the she-camel. He made "the command" (al-amr) something that is obeyed by way of figurative attribution in the judgment (al-majāz al-ḥukmī, a figurative usage in which the judgment is attributed to something other than its actual agent), while what is meant is the one who commands (al-āmir). This is every sentence in which the judgment it conveys is taken out of its proper place in the intellect through some kind of interpretation (ta'wil), like their saying "the spring grew the herbage."

﴿Those who spread corruption in the earth﴾ through injustice and disbelief, ﴿and do not set things right﴾ through faith and justice. The meaning is that their corruption is unmixed, with no trace of righteousness in it, unlike the condition of some corrupters whose corruption is mingled with some righteousness.

Their saying: ﴿You are only one of those who have been bewitched.﴾ Al-musahharun (those bewitched) is one who has been bewitched so much that his reason has been overcome. It was also said that it derives from al-sahr (the windpipe, lungs), meaning that he is a mere human being.
You are nothing but a human like us, so bring a sign, if you are among the truthful, in your claim to prophethood.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 155:

﴿He said: This is a she-camel; she has a share of water﴾ (a portion of the water), so do not crowd her out of it. ﴿And for you is a share of a known day﴾ in which she will not crowd you. It is narrated that they said: "We want a pregnant she-camel (ʿusharāʾ, one in her tenth month) to come out of this rock and give birth to a young camel (saqb)." So Ṣāliḥ began to reflect, and Jibrīl said to him: "Pray two rakʿahs and ask your Lord for the she-camel." He did so, and the she-camel came out and gave birth to a young one like her in size. Her chest was sixty cubits (dhirāʿ) wide. When it was her day to drink, she drank all of their water, and when it was their day to drink, she did not drink water on it. This is evidence for the permissibility of muhaayaʾa (the alternating arrangement of shares, i.e., taking turns), because His words ﴿She has a share of water, and for you is a share of a known day﴾ are of the kind of muhaayaʾat (alternating arrangements).

"And do not touch her with harm, lest there seize you the punishment of a great day."
(Qur'an 26:156)

With striking, or hamstringing, or otherwise.

"Lest there seize you the punishment of a great day": He described the day as great because the punishment descends upon it. Describing the day with greatness is more eloquent than describing the punishment itself, because when a time is made great by reason of what occurs in it, its effect in greatness is all the more intense.

"So they hamstrung her." It was Qudar who hamstrung her, but they were all content with it, so it was attributed to them. It is related that the one who hamstrung her said, "I will not hamstring her until you all are pleased [with it]." So they would enter upon the women in their seclusion and say, "Are you pleased?" and she would say, "Yes." And likewise their children. "Then they became regretful" over hamstringing her, out of fear of the descent of the punishment upon them. It was the regret of repentance, or they regretted when regret no longer benefits, and that was at the moment of witnessing the punishment, or [they regretted] over abandoning offspring.
﴿So the punishment seized them﴾, the one mentioned earlier. ﴿Surely in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers﴾.

Verse 165 of Surah al-Shu'ara' (26): ﴿Do you approach the males among the worlds?﴾

Al-Nasafi: He meant by "the worlds" the people. "Do you have intercourse with the males of mankind, despite the abundance of females? Or do you, from among all the others of the worlds, approach males, meaning: you are singled out for this abomination?" And "the worlds," on this reading, means everything among the animals that is mated with.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 166:

﴿And leave what your Lord has created for you of your spouses﴾. "Min" (from) is either explanatory of "what He created" or partitive. What is meant by "what He created" is the permissible part of them (the spouses), and they used to do the like with their wives. In this is evidence for the prohibition of anal intercourse with wives and female slaves, and whoever permitted it has erred a grave error. ﴿Nay, but you are a people transgressing﴾. Al-'Adi (the transgressor) is one who oversteps in his wrongdoing, going beyond the limit in it. That is: nay, you are a people deserving to be described as aggressors, in that you have committed such a grave act.

"They said, 'If you do not desist, O Lut, from your denunciation of us and your condemnation of our affair, you will surely be among those expelled'" ﴿لَتَكُونَنَّ مِنَ المُخْرَجِينَ﴾ — that is, among those in the category of those whom we have expelled from amongst us and driven out of our land. And perhaps they used to expel whoever they expelled in the worst condition.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 168:

﴿He said: "Indeed, I am, of your deed, among those who hate (it)."﴾ His saying "min al-qaline" (among those who hate) is more emphatic than saying "qali" (a hater). Your saying "fulan min al-ʿulama'" (so-and-so is among the scholars) is more emphatic than your saying "fulan ʿalim" (so-and-so is a scholar), because you are testifying that he shares with them in knowledge. Al-qila (hatred) is intense hatred, as though it is a hatred that burns (yaqli) the heart and the liver. And in it there is evidence of the greatness of disobedience, because his hatred of it stems from religion.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 169:

﴿Lord, deliver me and my family from what they do.﴾ That is, from the punishment for their deeds.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 170:

﴿So We saved him and his family, all of them.﴾ He means: his daughters and those who believed with him.

ۚ﴿Except an old woman﴾ — she was the wife of Lot, and she was content with that (deed). Contentment with sin is treated as the same as committing it. The exception of the disbelieving woman from "the family" (who were believers) is because of their sharing in this sin, even though she did not share with them in faith. ﴿Among those who remained behind﴾ is a qualifier of her, meaning: among those left behind in the punishment, so she was not saved from it. In the language, "al-ghabir" means "the remaining," as if it were said: "except an old woman, remaining" — i.e., her remaining (to be destined) was decreed, since remaining was not an attribute of hers at the time of their deliverance. (p-579)

Then We destroyed the others. (Q. 26:172)

What is meant by their destruction is that they were annihilated.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 173:

﴿And We rained down upon them a rain﴾. From Qatadah: God rained stones from the sky upon the scoundrels of the people, and God destroyed them. It was also said: He was not content with the overturning until He sent after it a rain of stones. ﴿Evil is﴾: its agent (fa'il) is ﴿the rain of those who were warned﴾, and the object of blame (al-makhsus bil-dhamm), which is "their rain," is omitted. By "those who were warned" he did not mean a specific people by name; rather, the intended meaning is the category of disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 176:

﴿The companions of the thicket (al-Aykah) denied the messengers.﴾

With the hamza and the kasra (read as "al-Aykah" with hamza and a kasra on the lam area, i.e. as the reading of the majority), it is a thicket (ghidah), which grows lush trees. This is related from al-Khalil. "Laykah" is the reading of the people of the Hijaz and Syria, and likewise in Surah Sad it is the name of a place. It is said: the companions of the thicket were the people of Madyan, who sought refuge in a thicket when the heat pressed upon them. The more correct view is that they were other than them: they settled in a specific thicket in the desert, and most of their trees were the doum palm (al-muql). The evidence is that here it does not say "their brother Shu'ayb," because he was not of their lineage, but rather of the lineage of the people of Madyan. Thus in the hadith: "Shu'ayb, brother of Madyan, was sent to them and to the companions of the thicket."

﴿the messengers.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 181:

﴿Give full measure﴾: complete it. ﴿And do not be among those who cause loss﴾: do not diminish people's rights. So full measure (al-kayl wafin) is commanded, and short measure (tatfif) is forbidden, while excess (za'id) is left unmentioned; leaving it unmentioned is evidence that if one does it, he has done well, and if he does not do it, there is no blame upon him. (p. 580)

﴿And weigh with the true balance﴾. With a kasra on the qaf, read by the Kufans except Abu Bakr. The word means the balance (al-mizan) or the steelyard (al-qabban). If it derives from al-qist, meaning justice, and its middle radical is doubled, its morphological pattern is fi'las. Otherwise it is quadriliteral (ruba'i).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 183:

﴿And do not deprive the people of their things﴾. It is said: "bakhastuhu haqqahu" (I deprived him of his right) when you diminish it for him. ﴿Their things﴾: their dirhams and their dinars, by clipping their edges. ﴿And do not commit abuse in the earth, causing corruption﴾: and do not exaggerate in corrupting them, such as highway robbery, raiding, and destroying crops. They used to do this, so they were forbidden from it. It is said: "atha fi al-ard" (he committed abuse in the land) when he caused corruption, and "athiya fi al-ard" is a dialectal variant of "atha'a" (the root meaning as in "athiya").

﴿And fear Him who created you and the previous generations﴾. "The previous generations" (al-Jibillah) is coordinated with "you" (kum): that is, fear Him who created you and created the previous generations, ﴿the former ones﴾, those who passed on.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 186:

﴿You are only a human being like us﴾ Here the particle waw (wa) is introduced to convey two meanings, both of which are incompatible with prophethood in their view: sorcery (al-tasḥīr) and humanity (al-basharīyah). In the story of Thamud, it was omitted in order to convey one meaning only, namely that he is one who has been bewitched (musaḥḥar). Then he affirmed, by his being a human like them. ﴿And indeed we think you are among the liars﴾ Inna is the light (mukhaffafah) form of the heavy (thaqīlah) inna, and the lam was introduced to distinguish it from the negative (nāfiyah) inna. The two were differentiated with the verb of thinking (fi'l al-zann) and its second object, because their original usage is that they be distinguished with the subject and predicate (al-mubtada' wa'l-khabar), as in your saying: inna Zaydan la-munṭaliqun (indeed Zayd is certainly leaving). Since kāna and ẓanantu belong to the same category as the subject-predicate construction (bāb al-mubtada' wa'l-khabar), this was applied to both categories, so it is said: in kāna Zaydun la-munṭaliqan (if Zayd was indeed leaving) and in ẓanantuhu la-munṭaliqan (if I thought him indeed leaving).

﴿So cause fragments to fall upon us from the sky﴾. Ḥafṣ reads كِسَفًا (*kisafan*) with a fatḥah on the sīn. "Both of them" (*wa-humā*) are plurals of كِسْفَةٌ (*kisfah*), which means "a piece" (*al-qiṭʿah*) [p. 581]. *Kasafahu* means "he cut it" (*qaṭaʿahu*). ﴿From the sky﴾: that is, from the clouds or the canopy. ﴿If you are of the truthful﴾: that is, if you are truthful that you are a prophet, then call upon God to cause fragments (*qiṭaʿan*) from the sky to fall upon us as a punishment.

"He said, 'My Lord is most knowing of what you do.'" (The reading ﴿قالَ رَبِّي﴾ with an open yā' is read by Ḥijāzī and Abū ʿAmr; the others read it with a sukūn on the yā'.) That is, God is most knowing of your deeds and of the punishment you deserve for them. So if He wills to punish you by dropping fragments from the sky, He will do it, and if He wills another punishment, the judgment and the will belong to Him.

﴿So they denied him, and the punishment of the Day of the Canopy seized them.﴾ It was a cloud that overshadowed them after it had withheld the wind from them, and they were tormented by heat for seven days. They gathered beneath it, seeking its shelter from the heat that had afflicted them, and it rained fire down upon them, and they were burned. ﴿Indeed, it was the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾

And indeed your Lord is surely the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful (﻿﴿وَإنَّ رَبَّكَ لَهو العَزِيزُ الرَحِيمُ﴾). In this surah He repeated, at the beginning and end of every story, what He repeated, in order to fix its meanings in the hearts, so that it would be more effective in admonition and deterrence. Also, each story in it is like a revelation on its own, and it contains the same lessons as the others, so it was fitting that it should begin with what its companions began with, and end with what they ended with.
And indeed it ﴿is﴾, that is, the Qur'an, ﴿a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾, sent down from Him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 193:

﴿Nazala bihi﴾ is read with a light (mukhaffafah) form, and the doer (al-fa'il) is ﴿al-ruhu al-amin﴾, i.e., Jibril (Gabriel), because he is trustworthy (amin) over the revelation in which there is life. Hijazi, Abu 'Amr, Zayd and Hafs, and others read it with the intensive (mushaddadah) form and the accusative on al-ruh, and the doer is Allah the Exalted, i.e., Allah made the Spirit descend with it. The ba' (bi) in both readings is for transitivity (lil-ta'diyah).

(p-582)

"Upon your heart": i.e., He made you memorize it, gave you understanding of it, and fixed it in your heart in a way that it would not be forgotten, like His saying ﴿We shall make you recite, so you will not forget﴾ [al-A'la: 6]. ﴿So that you may be among the warners﴾

**﴿in a clear Arabic tongue﴾**: in the dialect of Quraysh and Jurhum. **﴿clear﴾**: eloquent, and corrected of what the common people had distorted. The letter *bāʾ* (with) may be connected either to **"the warners"**, meaning: so that you may be among those who warned with this tongue, namely Hud, Salih, Shuʿayb and Ismaʿil, peace be upon them; or to **"sent down"**, meaning: He sent it down in a clear Arabic tongue so that you might warn with it. For if He had sent it down in a non-Arabic tongue, they would have turned away from it altogether and said, "What use is it to us to have something we do not understand?" The warning would then have been impossible.

In this second interpretation there is also the point that its being sent down in Arabic, which is your tongue and the tongue of your people, is a sending down upon your heart. This is because you understand it and make your people understand it. Had it been non-Arabic, it would have descended upon your hearing rather than your heart, since you would hear the sounds of letters without understanding or grasping their meanings.
