A person may know several languages, but when he is addressed in the language in which he was raised, his heart looks only at the meanings of the speech. If he is addressed in another language, his attention first falls on its words and only then on their meanings, even if he is skilled in it. This establishes that it descended upon his heart, since it descended in a clear Arabic tongue.

﴿And indeed it﴾ (that is, indeed the Qur'an) ﴿is in the Scriptures of the former peoples﴾. Meaning: its mention is established in all the heavenly books. It was also said that its meanings are found in them. This is evidence that the Qur'an remains the Qur'an when it is translated into a language other than Arabic. Therefore it is evidence for the permissibility of reciting the Qur'an in Persian during prayer (ṣalāh).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 197:

﴿, and was it not a sign for them﴾ Shami read "āyatun" as the subject (ism) of kāna, with its predicate (khabar) being ﴿that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it﴾, meaning the Qur'an, because its mention is present in the Torah. It was also said that the pronoun in "yakun" refers to the matter (ḍamīr al-qiṣṣa), and "āyatun" is the fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), while the subject (mubtada') is "an ya'lamahu", and the clause is the predicate of kāna. It was also said that kāna is complete (tāmmah), its agent (fā'il) is "āyatun", and "an ya'lamahu" is a substitute (badal) from it, or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: (p-583) "Did there not come about for them a sign?" Others read "yakun" with the masculine marker, and "āyatan" in the accusative as its predicate, and "an ya'lamahu" is the subject (ism), its estimated meaning being: "Or was it not a sign for them that the knowledge of the scholars of the Children of Israel [of it]..."

﴿the scholars of the Children of Israel﴾, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and others. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when it is recited to them, they say, "We believed in it; indeed it is the truth from our Lord. Indeed we were Muslims before it."﴾ [al-Qasas: 53]. In the Muṣḥaf, "ʿUlamā'u" was written with a wāw before the alif.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 198:

﴿And if We had sent it down upon some of the non-Arabs﴾ (al-A'jamin) is the plural of a'jam, which is one who cannot express himself clearly. Likewise al-a'jami, except that the addition of the nisba yaʾ (the yaʾ of relative adjectives) gives it added emphasis. And since whoever speaks in a language other than theirs, they do not understand his speech, they called him a'jam and a'jami, likening him to one who does not express himself clearly nor makes himself understood. Al-'ajami, who is of the stock of the 'Ajam, whether he expresses himself clearly or not, [is also so called]. Al-Hasan recited "al-a'jamiyyin," and it was said that "al-a'jamin" is a lightened form of "al-a'jamiyyin," as they said "al-ash'arun," meaning "al-ash'ariyyun," with the nisba yaʾ dropped. Were it not for this assumption, it would not be permissible to pluralize it with the sound masculine plural, because its feminine form is ʿajmaʾ.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 199:

﴿So he recited it to them, and they would not believe in it.﴾ The meaning is: We sent down the Qur'an upon a clear Arab man, and they understood it, recognised its eloquence, and that it is inimitable (mu'jiz). To this was added the agreement of the scholars of the People of the Book before him that the good news of its descent and its description were in their scriptures, and it contained its meanings and its stories. Through this it was established that it is from Allah and is not "fables of the ancients," as they claimed. Yet they did not believe in it; they called it poetry at one time and sorcery at another, and said, "This is nothing but the fabrication of Muhammad," upon him be blessings and peace. Had We sent it down upon some non-Arab who does not speak Arabic well, let alone being able to compose its like, and he had recited it to them in this inimitable form, they would have disbelieved in it just as they disbelieved, and they would have contrived an excuse for their denial and called it sorcery. Then He said.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 200:

﴿Thus We cause it to enter﴾

That is: We caused disbelief (takdhib, denial, or kufr, disbelief) to enter, which is the meaning of His words ﴿they would not believe in it﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 199], ﴿into the hearts of the criminals﴾, meaning the disbelievers whom We knew to have chosen disbelief and to persist in it. That is to say: We caused such an entering to enter into their hearts and established it there. Whatever is done to them, and in whatever manner their affair is arranged, there is no way for them to change from the disbelief and denial of it in which they are. As He said: ﴿And even if We had sent down to you a written scroll, and they had touched it with their hands, those who disbelieve would have said, "This is nothing but evident magic"﴾ [al-An'am: 7]. And this is our proof against the Mu'tazilah concerning the creation of the acts of the servants, both their good and their evil.

The position of His saying, ﴿They will not believe in it﴾ (referring to the Qur'an), after His saying ﴿We have caused it to enter into the hearts of the criminals﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 200], is the position of an elucidation and a summary. This is because it is brought to establish that it (the Qur'an) is denied and rejected in their hearts, so it follows what confirms this meaning: that they continue to deny it and reject it until they witness the threatened punishment. It may also be a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: We caused it to enter into their hearts while it was not believed in by them, ﴿until they see the painful punishment﴾. The intended meaning is witnessing the punishment at the time of death, and that will be the faith of despair, which does not benefit them.

[Qur'an 26:202] "So that it comes upon them suddenly, while they do not perceive it."

Al-Nasafi: "Suddenly" (fajʾatan), abruptly; "while they do not perceive" (wa-hum la yashʿurun) its coming.

﴿فَيَقُولُوا﴾ and ﴿فَيَأْتِيهِمْ﴾ are conjoined (معطوفان, *ma'tufan*) to ﴿يَرَوْا﴾ (they see), [so that they] ﴿say: Will we be given respite?﴾ They ask for reprieve and delay, even for the blink of an eye, but they are not granted it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 204:

﴿Will they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ This is a rebuke to them and a denunciation of their statement ﴿"Rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment."﴾ [al-Anfal: 32] and the like.
﴿Have you considered: if We let them enjoy [worldly comforts] for years﴾. It was said: these are the years of the duration of the world.
﴿Then there came to them what they had been promised﴾ of the punishment.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 207:

﴿Of what avail to them was what they were given enjoyment of﴾ in that (worldly) life for those years. The meaning is: their hastening of the punishment was only because of their belief that it would not occur and would not overtake them, and that they would be given enjoyment with long lives in safety and security. So Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then do they seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ out of wickedness, insolence, mockery, and reliance on long hope. Then He said: Suppose that the matter is as they believe, regarding their being given enjoyment and long life; yet when the threat overtakes them after that, what will the long length of their lives and the goodness of their livelihoods avail them at that time?

And it is related from Maymun ibn Mihran that he met al-Hasan during the circumambulation (tawaf), and he had long desired to meet him. He said: "Admonish me." Al-Hasan did not add to it beyond reciting this verse. Maymun said: "You have admonished and made it complete."

And it is related from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz that he used to recite it when he sat to judge (lil-hukm).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 208:

﴿And We did not destroy any town but that it had warners﴾ — messengers who warned them. The waw (واو, "and") was not placed before the clause after illa (إلا, "except/but") as in ﴿And We did not destroy any town but that it had a known decree﴾ [al-Hijr: 4], because the original form is the absence of the waw, since the clause is a qualifier (صِفَة, sifah) for "town" (قَرْيَة, qaryah); and when it is added, it is for emphasising the connection of the qualifier to the qualified (مَوْصُوف, mawsuf).

The word ﴿ذِكْرى﴾ is in the accusative (*manṣūb*) with the sense of *tadhkira* (a reminder), because *undhiru* (أُنْذِرُ) and *udhakkiru* (أُذَكِّرُ) are close in meaning. It is as if it had been said: "warning [them] as a reminder" (*mudhakkirūna tadhkiratan*). It may also be a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun in *mundhirūn*, meaning: "they warn them, [being] people of reminder" (*dhawī tadhkiratin*). Or it may be an object of purpose (*maf'ūl lahu*), meaning: "they warn for the sake of reminder and admonition." It may also be in the nominative, as the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*) in the sense of "this is a reminder," and the sentence is then parenthetical (*i'tirāḍiyya*). Or it may be a qualifier (*ṣifa*) in the sense of "warners who are possessors of reminder" (*dhawū dhikrā*). Or ﴿ذِكْرى﴾ may be linked to *ahlakna* (هْلَكْنا, "We destroyed") as an object of purpose. The meaning then is: "We did not destroy any town's people, being wrongdoers, except after We had established the proof against them by sending warners to them, so that their destruction would be a reminder and a lesson to others, so that they would not disobey as they disobeyed." ﴿And We were not wrongdoers﴾, so that We would destroy a people who were not wrongdoers.
When the polytheists said, "The devils are casting the Qur'an upon Muhammad (ﷺ)," it was sent down: ﴿The devils have not brought it down﴾ — that is, the Qur'an — ﴿the devils﴾.

"And it is not befitting for them, and they are not able to" — it does not become easy for them, and they are not capable of it.
﴿Indeed they are removed from hearing.﴾ They are surely prevented by the *shuhub* (shooting stars). (p-586)

"So do not invoke with Allah another deity, lest you be among those punished." The address of this prohibition is to someone other than him, by way of indirect warning and to stir him toward increasing sincerity (ikhlas).

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 214:**

﴿And warn your closest kinsfolk﴾. He singled them out to negate any accusation (of favoritism), since a person is lenient toward his own relatives; or so that they would know that he cannot avail them anything against Allah, and that salvation lies in following him, not in kinship (qurbah).

When it was revealed, he ascended al-Safa and called out to the nearest and then the next nearest, and said: "O Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib! O Banu Hashim! O Banu 'Abd Manaf! O 'Abbas, uncle of the Prophet! O Safiyyah, aunt of the Messenger of Allah! Indeed, I cannot avail you anything against Allah."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 215:

﴿And lower your wing﴾ meaning: soften your side, and be humble. Its origin is that when a bird wishes to descend to alight, it folds and lowers its wing, and when it wishes to rise up for flight, it raises its wing. So the lowering of the wing at the time of descent was made a metaphor (mathal) for humility and gentleness of the side. ﴿For those who follow you of the believers﴾, from your kinsfolk and others.

"Then if they disobey you" (﴿فَإنْ عَصَوْكَ﴾): that is, warn your people. If they follow you and obey you, then lower your wing to them (﴿فاخْفِضْ جَناحَكَ لَهم﴾). But if they disobey you and do not follow you, then disassociate yourself from them and from their deeds of polytheism (shirk) with Allah and other than Him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 217:

﴿And put your trust in the Almighty, the Most Merciful﴾. [He is] the One who subdues your enemies by His might and gives you victory over them by His mercy; He will suffice you against the evil of those among them, and others, who disobey you. Tawakkul (reliance, entrusting oneself to God): a man entrusting his affair to the one who controls his affair and is able to benefit or harm him. And they said: the one who relies (mutawakkil) is one who, when a matter befalls him, does not attempt to repel it from himself by means that are disobedience to God. And al-Junayd (may Allah be pleased with him) said: Tawakkul is that you turn wholly toward your Lord and turn wholly away from whatever is other than Him, for your need of Him is in both abodes. "Fa-tawakkal" (so put your trust) is read by Madani and Shami [readers] as a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "fa-qul" (so say) or "fa-la tadʿu" (so do not invoke).

(p-587)
﴿Who sees you when you stand [for prayer]﴾, [meaning, standing in] tahajjud (voluntary night prayer).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 219:

﴿And your turning about among those who prostrate﴾ means: and He sees your turning about among those who pray (al-musalliyin). He followed His being Merciful to His Messenger with that which is among the causes of mercy, namely the mention of what he used to do in the depth of the night: his standing for tahajjud (voluntary night prayer), and his turning about while scrutinizing the states of his Companions who performed tahajjud, so that he might observe them without their noticing, and know how they worship Allah and work for their Hereafter.

It has also been said that its meaning is: He sees you when you stand for prayer leading the people in congregation (jama'ah). "Your turning about among those who prostrate" then refers to your movement among them with your standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting when you lead them.

It is related from Muqatil that he asked Abu Hanifa: "Do you find congregational prayer (al-salat bi'l-jama'ah) in the Qur'an?" He replied: "It does not come to my mind." So he recited to him this verse.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 220:

﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing﴾ of what you say, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of what you intend and do. This eased for him the hardship of bearing the difficulties of the acts of worship, since he was informed of His seeing him, for there is no hardship upon one who knows that he acts in the sight of his Master. This is like His saying (in a hadith qudsi): "They bear what they bear for My sake, with My eye (watching)."

This was revealed in reply to the claim of the polytheists that the devils (shayatin) were casting the hearing (of the heavenly news) upon Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿Shall I inform you﴾ — that is, shall I tell you, O polytheists, upon whom the devils descend? Then he informed them, saying:

﴿Upon every lying, sinful one do the devils descend﴾ — the one who commits sins (al-athām). They are the soothsayers (al-kahanah) and the false prophets (al-mutanabbi'ah), such as Satih, Tulayhah and Musaylimah. Muhammad (ﷺ) reviles the liars and censures them, so how would the devils descend upon him?!

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 223:

﴿They cast the hearing﴾: they are the devils (shayatin), who used to listen to the Exalted Assembly (al-Mala' al-A'la) before they were barred by meteors. They would overhear some of what was spoken there, of the unseen matters they had glimpsed, and then they would inspire it to their associates (awliya'). And they cast [the hearing] as a ḥāl (a circumstantial clause), meaning: they descend as ones who cast the hearing (mulqina al-sam'); or it is a ṣifah (a descriptive qualifier) of every liar (affak), since it carries the sense of a plural, so it is in the genitive position (maḥall al-jarr). (p-588) Or it is an isti'naf (a resumptive, independent clause), so it has no grammatical position, as if it were said: "Why do they descend upon the liars?" and it was answered: "They do such-and-such." ﴿And most of them are liars﴾ in what they inspire to them, because they make them hear what they have not heard. It was also said: "They cast the hearing to their associates," meaning what is heard from the angels. It was said: "The liars cast the hearing to the devils and receive their revelation from them," or "they cast what is heard from the devils to people." And most liars are liars: they fabricate against the devils what they did not inspire to them. An affak is one who frequently utters falsehood (ifk), and this does not indicate that they speak only falsehood. The intent is that few of these liars speak truly regarding what they relate from the jinn, and most of them fabricate against him.

It is related from al-Hasan: "And all of them are liars." He distinguished between ﴿And indeed it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 192], ﴿Nor have the devils brought it down﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 210], and ﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 221], though they are sisters (akhawat, i.e., related passages). For when one separates them with verses that are not of them, then returns to them time and again, this indicates intense concern for them, just as when you speak a speech while there is preoccupation with something in your heart, so you repeat its mention and do not cease returning to it.

It was revealed concerning those who used to recite poetry and say: "We say just as Muhammad (ﷺ) says," and misguided people of their folk followed them, listening to their poems.

**Al-Nasafi, Madarik al-Tanzil, on Surah 26, verse 224:**

﴿Wa-al-shu‘arā'﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is ﴿yattabi‘uhumu al-ghāwūn﴾. That is: they are not followed in their falsehood, their lying, the tearing apart of people's honour, the slandering of human beings, and the praise of one who does not deserve praise. Such things are approved of only by the ghāwūn, that is, the foolish (al-sufahā'), or the transmitters (al-rāwūn), or the devils (al-shayāṭīn), or the polytheists (al-mushrikūn). Al-Zajjaj said: when a poet praises or satirises someone with what is not true, and a people love that and follow him, then they are the ghāwūn.

"Yattabi‘uhum" (﴿يَتْبَعُهُمُ﴾, with the verb form read as yattabi‘uhum): this reading is transmitted from Nafi‘.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 225:

﴿Have you not seen that they wander distractedly in every valley﴾ of speech ﴿and that they say what they do not do?﴾ The clause "that they" is the subject of ﴿in every valley they wander﴾; that is, in every kind of falsehood they speak, or in every idle and vain matter they plunge. The hā'im (wanderer) is one who goes off aimlessly with no destination, and this is an image of their going off into every path of speech and their deviation (i'tisāf), to the point that they prefer the most cowardly of people over ʿAntara (ʿAntarah) and the most miserly over Ḥātim (Ḥātim al-Ṭā'ī). From al-Farazdaq, that Sulayman ibn ʿAbd al-Malik heard his saying: (p-589)

Then they spent the night beside me, stretched out, and I spent the night unlocking the seals of the sealed wine-jar.

He said: "The prescribed punishment (ḥadd) is due upon you." He replied: "God has averted the prescribed punishment from me by His saying."
Quran 26:226: ﴿And that they say what they do not do.﴾ Here He described them as liars and as breaking promises, then He excepted the believing, righteous poets with His saying:

﴿Except for those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾, like ʿAbd Allah ibn Rawaha, Hassan ibn Thabit, Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr, and Kaʿb ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with them all. ﴿And remember Allah often﴾, meaning that the remembrance of Allah and the recitation of the Qur'an were more dominant among them than poetry. When they did compose poetry, they composed it on the Oneness of Allah (tawhid), the praise of Him, wisdom, admonition, asceticism (zuhd), good conduct (adab), the praise of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the Companions, the righteous of the Ummah, and similar matters, nothing in which is sinful. Abu Yazid said: "Much remembrance is not by number, nor by heedlessness, but by presence (of the heart)." ﴿And defended themselves﴾, and satirized, ﴿after they had been wronged﴾, meaning they answered the satire of those who satirized the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims. The most deserving of all people to be satirized are those who denied the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and satirized him. It is narrated from Kaʿb ibn Malik that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Satirize them, for by the One in whose hand is my soul, it is more painful to them than arrows." And he used to say to Hassan: "Say it, and the Holy Spirit is with you." He concluded the surah with what cuts the livers of those who reflect, which is His saying ﴿And those who have wronged will know﴾, along with its eloquent threat, His saying ﴿those who have wronged﴾ with its generality, and His saying ﴿what [sort of] return they will return to﴾ with its vagueness. Abu Bakr recited it to ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, when he appointed him (as caliph), and the predecessors used to admonish one another with it. Ibn ʿAta' said: "Let the one who turns away from Us know what he has missed from Us." The word ﴿أيَّ﴾ (ayya, "what sort of") is in the accusative, governed by ﴿يَنْقَلِبُونَ﴾ (yanqalibun, "they will return") as a verbal noun (masdar), not by ﴿يَعْلَمُ﴾ (yaʿlamu, "will know"), because interrogative particles are not governed by what precedes them. The meaning is: they will return with what sort of return. And Allah knows best.

It is narrated from al-Farazdaq that Sulayman ibn ʿAbd al-Malik heard his saying:
